concept.sub_category: Magic Squares — 5×5 Odd Order (Panchadasi / Extended Siamese)

examples.problem_statement: Construct a 5×5 magic square using the Extended Siamese method (Panchadasi). Numbers 1–25. Verify magic constant = 65.

solution.operation: Place 1 at the top-center cell (row 0, col 2)
solution.description: The Siamese method for any odd n starts with 1 at row 0, col (n-1)/2. For n=5: col = 2.

solution.operation: Place 2 diagonally up-right → (row 4, col 3) — wrap both
solution.description: Up from row 0 wraps to row 4; right from col 2 goes to col 3. Toroidal wrapping in both dimensions.
Up from row 4 → row 3; right from col 3 → col 4. Normal diagonal.
Up from row 3 → row 2; right from col 4 wraps to col 0. The cell (2,0) is empty, so place 4.
Up from row 2 → row 1; right from col 0 → col 1. Normal diagonal.

solution.operation: Target (0,2) occupied by 1 → drop DOWN to (2,1). Place 6.
solution.description: COLLISION: (0,2) already has 1. Drop down from (1,1) to (2,1). This is the same collision rule as in 3×3.

solution.operation: Continue placing 7–13 following the same rules
solution.description: 7→(0,0)→collision, drop→(3,1)... following the same diagonal+wrap+collision-drop pattern. Each number follows the identical algorithm.

solution.operation: Continue placing 8–19 following the same rules

solution.description: Each row sums to M = n(n²+1)/2 = 5×26/2 = 65.
Each column sums to 65.
Both main diagonals sum to 65. The center cell (2,2) = 13 = (n²+1)/2 = 26/2.

solution.operation: ASCII verification of the completed 5×5 Panchadasi magic square
solution.description: Complete verification. The 5×5 square has 12 lines (5 rows + 5 columns + 2 diagonals) all summing to 65.

solution.operation: PATTERN: Center cell and symmetric properties
solution.description: Every pair of cells symmetric about the center sums to n²+1 = 26. This is a fundamental property of odd-order magic squares constructed by the Siamese method.

key_reminders: {'point': 'The Siamese method for 5×5 uses the EXACT same rules as 3×3 — only the grid is larger.'}
{'point': 'Starting position: row 0, col (n-1)/2 = 2. This generalizes to any odd n.'}
{'point': 'Magic constant: M = n(n²+1)/2 = 5×26/2 = 65.'}
{'point': "Center cell = (n²+1)/2 = 13. It's always the arithmetic mean of 1 and n²."}
{'point': "Opposite cell pairs sum to n²+1 = 26. This is the 'complement' property."}
{'point': 'The 5×5 square has 12 independent lines (5R + 5C + 2D) — all must equal 65.'}

examples.problem_statement: Represent the number 7 using the Roman additive principle.

solution.description: Roman numerals use specific letters to represent values. The additive principle means values are added when a smaller numeral follows a larger one.
We can express 7 as the sum of 5 and two 1s.
In Roman numerals, V represents 5 and I represents 1.
Since the smaller numerals (I) come after the larger numeral (V), we add them together: 5 + 1 + 1 = 7.
Confirming that VII correctly represents 7 using the additive principle.

examples.problem_statement: Represent the number 38 using Roman digits.

solution.description: Combine Roman digits additively: 30 (XXX) + 5 (V) + 3 (III).

examples.problem_statement: Represent the number 345 using the Greek alphabetic system.

solution.description: Substitute Greek letters for numbers: 300 (Τ), 40 (Μ), 5 (Ε).

examples.problem_statement: Represent the number 2,342 using the Mesopotamian (Mari) hybrid notation.

solution.description: The Mari notation mixes repetition with named ranks. Repeat the unit sign to give the count for each rank and attach the rank word: two thousands, three hundreds, four tens and two loose units, which assembles to 2,342.

examples.problem_statement: Represent the number 2,342 using the Chinese multiplicative notation.

solution.description: Chinese notation is multiplicative rather than additive, so each digit sign is written immediately before the rank word it multiplies. Transcribing 2,342 sign by sign gives 2 thousand, 3 hundred, 4 ten, 2.

common_mistakes: Slipping into the subtractive form when writing 38; the additive principle used here spells 8 as V I I I, never as I I X.
Reading the Greek answer T M E as a place-value numeral. T, M and E are three separate symbols worth 300, 40 and 5, not digits sitting in columns.
Reading the Chinese form 2 1000 3 100 4 10 2 additively. The digit in front of each rank word multiplies it, so the leading pair is 2 times 1000, not 2 plus 1000.

examples.problem_statement: Determine the implied accuracy of the statement that a dinosaur is '70 million' years old.

solution.operation: Understand significant figures in scientific notation
solution.description: Writing 70 million in scientific notation as 7.0 times 10 to the seventh makes the claimed precision visible. Two significant figures are quoted, and the zero after the decimal point is asserted as measured rather than as padding.

solution.operation: Identify the place value of the last significant digit
solution.description: Locate the last significant digit. It is the zero standing immediately after the 7, and in 70,000,000 that position is the millions place. This place, not the whole string of trailing zeros, fixes how finely the age is quoted.

A figure quoted without stated error bars is read as accurate to half a unit of its last significant place. Half of one million is 0.5 times 10 to the sixth, so the implied slack is 500,000 years either way.
Apply that slack to the stated value: 70,000,000 plus or minus 500,000. The true age is being claimed to lie somewhere between 69,500,000 and 70,500,000 years.

solution.operation: Express the precision in appropriate units
solution.description: Restate the precision in the units the claim itself uses. Because the last significant digit counts millions, the range is half a million years wide on each side, or plus or minus 0.5 million.

Compare the two readings. Plus or minus 10 million would be right only if 70 million carried a single significant figure, 7 times 10 to the seventh. Two significant figures were quoted, so plus or minus 0.5 million is the accuracy the statement actually implies.

examples.answer: This value is implicitly understood to within 0.5 million years.

examples.problem_statement: Compare the implied accuracy of the population figures 39,000,000 and 39,452,000.

solution.operation: Apply the rule: accuracy is given by the last non-zero digit starting from the right.
solution.description: Read each figure from the right until the first non-zero digit. In 39,000,000 that digit is the 9 in the millions place; in 39,452,000 it is the 2 in the thousands place. The second figure is pinned down a thousand times more finely, so it is good to about a thousand while the first is only good to about a million.

examples.answer: 39,000,000 is correct to within a million, whereas 39,452,000 is correct to give or take a thousand.

common_mistakes: Assuming 39,000,000 is an exact count because it ends in zeros; those zeros are placeholders, not measured digits.
Counting every trailing zero of 70 million as significant and claiming the dinosaur's age is known to the nearest year.
Quoting the slack as a whole unit of the last significant place, plus or minus 1 million, instead of half a unit, plus or minus 0.5 million.

examples.problem_statement: A bet on the first digit of a random number in a book: if the digit is 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, or 9, you win ten dollars. If it is 1, 2, or 3, the opponent wins ten dollars. Is this a good bet?

solution.description: Benford's Law states that in many naturally occurring number sets, the probability of a number starting with digit d is given by this formula.
Sum the probabilities for digits 1, 2, and 3 using Benford's Law.
The total probability must sum to 1, so subtract P(1,2,3) from 1.

solution.operation: Calculate expected value for the bet
solution.description: Multiply each outcome by its probability and sum them to find the expected value.
A negative expected value means the bet is unfavorable for the person choosing digits 4-9.

examples.answer: The bet is a loser for the person choosing digits 4-9.

common_mistakes: Assuming every leading digit is equally likely, which would make 4 through 9 win six times out of nine; Benford's law leaves them only about 40 percent.
Counting how many digits sit on each side of the bet instead of adding their probabilities. Digits 1, 2 and 3 are fewer in number but together carry about 60 percent of the leading positions.
Reading the expected value of minus 2.04 dollars as the outcome of a single draw; it is the average per bet, and any one draw still pays either plus or minus ten dollars.

examples.problem_statement: How to refer to numbers beyond 3?

solution.result: n = d_k b^k + d_{k-1} b^{k-1} + \cdots + d_1 b^1 + d_0 b^0
solution.description: Any positive integer can be expressed in a given base $b$ using digits $d_i$ where $0 \le d_i < b$.
For a base $b$, the allowable digits are from 0 up to $b-1$. For bases greater than 3, the digit 3 is always allowed, but digits 4, 5, etc., are only allowed if they are less than $b$.

solution.operation: Numbers up to 3 are single-digit in any base $b \ge 4$
solution.description: Since 3 < b for any base b ≥ 4, the number 3 is represented by the single digit '3'.
In base 4, the digit 4 is not allowed (digits only 0-3). The number 4 is one full group of 4 and zero units, hence written as '10'.
In base 5, digits 0-4 are allowed, so 4 is still a single digit. Numbers exceeding 4 require two digits. , and

solution.result: \text{If } n > b-1, \text{ then the representation uses at least two digits.}
solution.description: The maximum single-digit number in base b is b-1. Any number greater than b-1 will occupy a higher place value. So to refer to numbers beyond 3 in any base b > 3, we use positional notation with multiple digits.

examples.answer: In base systems, numbers beyond 3 are represented using multiple digits, where each digit's place value is a power of the base. For base b > 3, digits range from 0 to b-1. Numbers greater than b-1 require two or more digits. For example, in base 4, the number 4 is written as 10 (one four and zero ones). In base 5, 4 is still a single digit (4), but 5 is written as 10. The statement in the current answer is incorrect; it is a mathematical concept of positional notation.

solution.description: We begin with the first addend in the expression.
We are adding 2 to the first number.

solution.operation: Count forward by the second number
solution.description: Starting from 4, count forward 2 units: 4 to 5 (first count), 5 to 6 (second count).
On a number line, starting at 4 and moving 2 units to the right lands on 6.
This is a basic addition fact that should be memorized.
Adding 4 to 2 means four counting steps, but 4 plus 2 means only two. Because addition is commutative the order can be swapped, so start from the larger number 4 and count on 2 to land on 6.
The 8 is two short of a round ten, so split the 4 into the piece that fills that gap and the remainder: 4 becomes 2 plus 2.
Add the first piece to reach the round number: 8 plus 2 makes 10, a value that is easy to hold in mind while the rest of the sum is finished.
Add the leftover 2 to that ten. Ten plus 2 is 12, so 8 plus 4 equals 12.
Only 2 is being taken away, so counting backward is the short route. From 8 step back twice, 8 to 7 and 7 to 6, which leaves 6.
Here 6 is being taken away, and six backward steps is a long walk. Turn the subtraction around and count up from 6 to the 8 instead: 6 to 7 and 7 to 8 is two steps, so 8 minus 6 is 2.

key_reminders: {'point': "The text identifies an 'optimal choice' rule for subtraction: 'The optimal choice is dictated by the size of the number to be subtracted."}

Stopping at the round ten when bridging 8 plus 4 and answering 10, having forgotten the second half of the split 4.
Counting back six times for 8 minus 6 and losing track, when counting up from 6 to 8 takes only two steps.

examples.problem_statement: Charlie David works on Albert Bruno Avenue.

solution.description: In the NATO phonetic alphabet, 'Charlie' stands for the letter 'C'.
The letter 'C' is the 3rd letter of the English alphabet, so it corresponds to the number 3.
Similarly, 'David' stands for the letter 'D' in the NATO phonetic alphabet.

solution.operation: Convert second letter to numerical position
solution.description: The letter 'D' is the 4th letter of the alphabet, so it corresponds to the number 4.
The phrase 'works on' in this context implies an arithmetic operation, typically multiplication (as suggested by the term 'professional address' indicating an operation).
Multiplying the two numbers yields 12, which is the final result.

examples.problem_statement: Charlie George works on Bruno Albert Avenue.

solution.description: Decode the two personal names first: Charlie is C, the 3rd letter, and George is G, the 7th, so the pair stands for 3 and 7. The avenue name carries the answer the same way, Bruno then Albert giving B then A, that is 2 then 1, so the product read off the address is 21.

examples.problem_statement: George Ernie works on Charlie Ernie Avenue.

solution.description: George is G, the 7th letter, and Ernie is E, the 5th, so the names supply the factors 7 and 5. Charlie Ernie Avenue decodes as C then E, that is 3 then 5, and the address therefore states the product 35.
